big: Rohan never told his UK tax office about his Indian rent, assuming India's tax was enough. His home country taxes world income. A letter arrived two years later, with interest and a penalty.

lines: I paid tax in India. Is that all?
Not necessarily. Your country of residence may tax worldwide income. Declare it there, keep your records, and ask a qualified adviser when rules in two countries meet.

rows: Declare your countries of tax residence to banks and fund houses
Declare Indian income where you live, as that country may tax it
Save statements, TDS certificates and remittance proofs every year
Ask a qualified adviser when two countries' rules meet
note: Rules change, so check the current rule with your bank or a qualified adviser.

title: Staying compliant
stops: Declare Indian income where you live too
One country's tax always covers the other

q: Meena earns rent in India. Where should she declare it?
opts: Nowhere, since it is only rent
In India and where she lives
Only on her social media page
Only to a close friend of hers
why: Not declaring is a legal risk with penalties.
Both countries may need to know, and credit can be claimed.
Social media is not a tax authority of any country.
A friend is not a tax authority of any country.

q: A bank gives Rohan a form to state his countries of tax residence. What is it?
why: It declares in which countries he is a tax resident.
It is not a loan form, but a residency declaration.
It is not a gift form, but a residency declaration.
It is not a lottery form, but a residency declaration.

q: Which habit helps at tax time?
opts: Throwing every single paper away at once
Keeping no records of any kind
Changing the name on the papers
why: Throwing papers away loses the proof that is needed.
Having no records means having no proof for claims.
Records support claims for credit or refund later.
Changing names causes mismatches in the records.

q: When rules of two countries interact, what is wise?
opts: Make a guess and hope it works
Ask a stranger on an online forum
Ignore the problem until it grows
why: Guessing is risky when two countries' laws are involved.
A stranger online may be wrong about the rules.
Ignoring it may bring penalties and interest later.
The answer depends on facts, so an adviser helps.

pts: Declare Indian income where you live too.
Self-certify your tax residence, and keep records every year.
